definition: Symbolism means the use of images, objects, or actions to stand for larger ideas — a wilting orchid carrying a family's decline, a storm carrying trouble to come.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word symbolism. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know symbolism should be able to work it out from your sentence.

An undertone is fainter than symbolism: it lets a second meaning hum quietly beneath a scene, while symbolism openly hands objects a larger idea to carry.
Allegory goes further than symbolism: symbolism loads certain images with larger meaning, but an allegory commits the entire story, start to finish, to standing for another one.

Allegory means a story whose entire surface maps onto a second, hidden story — every character and event a stand-in from first page to last. Symbolism is more selective: certain images carry larger ideas, while the rest of the work stays simply itself.
Imagery means language that appeals to the senses — it makes you see, hear, and smell the scene. Symbolism goes a step further: it takes what you see and makes it stand for something more.

Metaphor means a figure of speech that directly calls one thing another, made once in passing — 'the road was a ribbon.' Symbolism is the wider practice of loading objects and actions with meaning across a whole work.

In the mural above the courthouse steps, the painter loaded every corner with symbolism: broken chains for the end of the old regime, an unhooded falcon for the freed press, and scales tipping toward a single feather for mercy outweighing gold.
Chains, falcon, scales — none of them matters as a mere object; each stands for a larger idea.
Meaning carried by images in that way is exactly what symbolism is.

Symbolism is the word for the practice as a whole; a single stand-in is a symbol.

SAT passages reward keeping the family straight: imagery appeals to the senses, a metaphor makes one direct comparison, symbolism makes objects carry ideas, and an allegory commits the entire story to a second meaning.
Outside literature the word covers gestures too — flying a flag at half-mast is pure symbolism, an action that exists to stand for grief.

When the seniors unveiled their graduation mural, half the school saw only a mountain road at dawn.
The road forked exactly at the mural's center; the guardrail was broken at one fork and mended at the other; a small paper boat rode the storm drain in the corner, headed off the wall.
None of it was labeled, but none of it was accidental — the painters had loaded the picture with symbolism, letting objects say what a banner could not.
The fork was the choice every graduate faced; the mended rail, the friends who catch you; the paper boat, everyone about to be carried somewhere new.
At the dedication, the principal simply pointed at the boat and said, 'That one's mine too.'
